Pygmy rockfish (Sebastes wilsoni) is a small-bodied scorpaenid that inhabits deep rocky reefs along the Pacific coast of North America. Field surveys indicate that the maximum recorded total length for this species is 23 centimeters [Li = 23 centimeters], a size that places it among the smaller members of the genus Sebastes. At the onset of reproductive maturity, individuals typically measure around 10 centimeters [Lp = around 10 centimeters] in total length, a threshold that appears to be reached after several years of slow, steady growth in the cold waters of the continental slope. The mass of an individual that has just attained this milestone is approximately 12.3 grams [Wwp = approximately 12.3 grams], reflecting the modest body size of maturing pygmy rockfish. These values, derived from extensive trawl surveys and otolith-based growth analyses, provide a reliable baseline for understanding the life-history strategy of this species in relation to its congener Sebastes hopkinsi.

Reproductive output in Pygmy rockfish has been estimated indirectly by scaling fecundity data from Sebastes hopkinsi, which produces approximately 39,000 oocytes at a length of 29 centimeters. Applying a cubic scaling relationship to the 23-centimeter ultimate length of S. wilsoni suggests a batch fecundity of approximately 19,000 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 19,000 eggs per spawning event], with spawning occurring roughly once per year [F_R_i = roughly once per year]. At a stable environmental temperature of 6.4 °C [T = 6.4 °C], these values together imply a maximum daily reproductive rate of approximately 52 eggs per day. These estimates are accompanied by the observation that the fertilized ova of this viviparous species measure approximately 0.8 millimeters in diameter. From this egg diameter, the calculated wet weight of a newly extruded, yolk-laden neonate is about 0.000268 grams [Wwb = about 0.000268 grams], an extremely small initial mass that underscores the high degree of maternal investment in a relatively altricial larval stage.

The maximum lifespan of Pygmy rockfish has been documented through otolith annulus counts conducted on specimens collected from the Gulf of Alaska and the Bering Sea. Under the prevailing thermal conditions of their deep-water habitat, which typically average 6.4 °C [T = 6.4 °C], the oldest individual recorded reached an age of approximately 26 years [am = approximately 26 years]. This considerable longevity is typical of many rockfish species and reflects a life-history strategy characterized by slow growth, late maturity, and extended reproductive lifespans. The combination of a small ultimate body size with such a prolonged lifespan is relatively unusual among teleosts and points to a low-mortality environment where steady, year-round nutrient input supports gradual somatic accumulation. The specific temperature dependence of this demographic parameter is notable, as the 6.4 °C mean annual temperature in these habitats likely contributes to the depressed metabolic rates that allow such extended survival.

In terms of adult body mass, the asymptotic or ultimate wet weight of Pygmy rockfish has been modeled from a length-weight relationship derived from the species' maximum length of 23 centimeters [Li = 23 centimeters]. Applying a standard power-law equation with a coefficient of 0.01000 and an exponent of 3.09 yields an estimated ultimate wet weight of 161 grams [Wwi = 161 grams]. This value aligns well with the few direct weight measurements available from large, presumably old individuals collected during deep-water research cruises. The body mass at the point of reproductive maturation, based analogously on the length at puberty of 10 centimeters, is estimated at 12.3 grams [Wwp = 12.3 grams], a figure that can be compared to that of other small-bodied rockfishes from similar thermal regimes. These two mass-related parameters — a 161-gram adult asymptote (161 grams) [Wwi = 161 grams] and a pubertal mass of 12.3 grams [Wwp = 12.3 grams] — together define a species with a narrow size window for reproductive activity.

Sexual maturation in Pygmy rockfish is marked by the first successful parturition event, which occurs after an extended period of juvenile development in the cold benthic environment. Under the typical temperature regime of 6.4 °C [T = 6.4 °C], field observations suggest that first reproduction takes place approximately 6 years after hatching [tR = 6 years after hatching]. This substantial delay before reproductive output begins is characteristic of the genus and is likely driven by the need to accumulate sufficient somatic reserves at the prevailing low temperature in their deep habitat. The species' iteroparous strategy, combined with a maximum recorded longevity of 26 years [am = 26 years] under the same thermal conditions, allows for numerous reproductive cycles over the adult lifespan at a temperature of 6.4 °C [T = 6.4 °C]. The 23-centimeter maximum length (23 centimeters) [Li = 23 centimeters] places this species among the smallest in the genus Sebastes, while the pubertal mass of 12.3 grams [Wwp = 12.3 grams] indicates a relatively low energetic investment threshold for entering the reproductive population.
